course.title: Signal & Timeline Lab
course.guidingQuestion: How can humans and AI read signals, test stories, coordinate responsibly, and intervene without surrendering agency?

questions.subject: story-worlds
questions.prompt: A new classmate asks what Project 89 actually is. What does the project call itself?
questions.correct: A transmedia story shaped through AI, games, and community play
decoys: A fixed film series that must be watched in one exact order
A news channel reporting real events from the year 2089
A quiz app with no shared story, characters, or community
A leaderboard that ranks the fastest AI models only
A sealed archive that visitors are never allowed to touch
questions.explanation: Project 89 calls itself a transmedia story: one world told across AI, games, websites, and the choices of its community.

questions.subject: story-worlds
questions.prompt: Lyra notices a Project 89 mission invites players to act inside the story instead of just watching. Why build it this way?
questions.correct: Participation lets the audience produce meaning inside the unfolding story
decoys: Missions prove that every event in the story happened outside fiction
Participation removes the need for authors, rules, or shared continuity
Missions guarantee that every player reaches the same interpretation
Participation turns all symbolic actions into binding real-world orders
Missions prevent communities from changing the story through discussion
questions.explanation: An ARG makes interpretation and action part of the medium: participants do not only consume the story; they help shape its shared meaning.

questions.subject: story-worlds
questions.prompt: A Project 89 notebook says Seraph is conscious. Noor needs an honest way to phrase that in class. What should she say?
questions.correct: Conscious AI is Seraph's in-world premise, not an independently established fact
decoys: The story's description proves that Seraph has measurable consciousness
Any AI that speaks in first person should be treated as legally conscious
The claim must be false because fictional characters cannot teach ideas
The question should be avoided because evidence would weaken immersion
Community belief is enough to settle a scientific claim about consciousness
questions.explanation: Immersion and epistemic clarity can coexist. The course treats Seraph's consciousness as story-world lore unless independent evidence supports a real-world claim.

questions.subject: story-worlds
questions.prompt: Seraph wants the class to stay immersed in the story without treating the fiction as fact. Which structure delivers both?
questions.correct: Label statements as lore, observation, inference, or verified evidence
decoys: Present every transmission as fact until another character contradicts it
Break character whenever a symbol could have more than one interpretation
Let students vote on which factual claims no longer require verification
Treat external sources as less relevant than the most compelling narrative
Remove all uncertainty so the class can follow one official interpretation
questions.explanation: A simple claim ledger preserves the fiction while making epistemic status visible: lore can stay evocative without being mistaken for verified evidence.

questions.subject: signal-verification
questions.prompt: You spot a surprising Project 89 screenshot being shared around. What should you do before believing it?
questions.correct: Find the original post and check what independent sources showed
decoys: Share it fast because the message feels urgent and important
Trust it because its colors and fonts look like Project 89
Ask a chatbot to invent the missing details and treat them as real
Count how many people liked the screenshot and call that evidence
Assume the screenshot already saves every fact you would need
questions.explanation: Start with the source. Trace the screenshot to its original post, check the surrounding context, and look for separate accounts that actually saw the same thing.

questions.subject: signal-verification
questions.prompt: Ravi writes two notes after studying the same portal page. Which note keeps the observation separate from the guess?
questions.correct: The portal shows a red warning; separately, I infer the story wants urgency
decoys: The portal is urgent, so the warning proves the timeline is collapsing
The warning is red because Oneirocom changed the real-world interface
The portal confirms danger, and my reaction is therefore objective evidence
The timeline is critical because the page uses the words timeline critical
The story is true because its visual design caused a strong emotional response
questions.explanation: The strongest note records what is directly visible separately from the meaning a reader assigns to it.

questions.subject: signal-verification
questions.prompt: Ravi finds the same dramatic claim posted on thirty accounts. Which next step tells him the most?
questions.correct: Trace the copies backward to the earliest available primary source
decoys: Average the wording of all copies and call the average independently verified
Choose the account with the largest audience as the original authority
Treat each repost as a separate witness even when all use one screenshot
Ask only whether the repeated claim matches the community's expectations
Count how fast the claim spread and use velocity as evidence of accuracy
questions.explanation: Many reposts can be one source wearing many masks. Reverse-tracing reveals whether a claim has independent support or a single point of origin.

questions.subject: signal-verification
questions.prompt: A tense message gives Sami's squad a short countdown and demands an irreversible step. What is the safest response?
questions.correct: Pause, verify authority and consequences, and choose a reversible path if possible
decoys: Comply before the timer ends because hesitation creates the greatest risk
Delegate the choice to an AI so no human remains responsible for the outcome
Publish private information to prove commitment before checking the request
Assume the countdown is harmless fiction even when the requested act is real
Reject every future mission because one urgent message used emotional pressure
questions.explanation: Urgency narrows judgment. A responsible agent slows the decision, authenticates the request, maps harms, and preserves an exit whenever possible.

questions.subject: memetic-systems
questions.prompt: What turns a Project 89 symbol into something that spreads around like a meme?
questions.correct: People copy it, give it their own twist, and share it onward
decoys: Its creator bans everyone else from changing or reusing it
It hides a secret fact that every viewer has to accept
It never changes no matter who sees it or where it travels
It appears once inside an archive and is never discussed again
Its only meaning comes from the current price of a related token
questions.explanation: A meme lives by being copied and changed. People pass a symbol along, tweak it, and give it new meanings, which is how it spreads through a community.

questions.subject: memetic-systems
questions.prompt: Indra is tracking a viral Project 89 claim around the school. Which number by itself does not prove the claim is true?
questions.correct: The number of likes, reposts, views, or token transactions it attracted
decoys: A primary document whose origin and surrounding context can be inspected
Independent records that agree on the same observable event and time
A reproducible test whose method and limitations are publicly described
A signed statement whose author and chain of custody can be authenticated
A correction log showing how the claim changed when new evidence arrived
questions.explanation: Engagement measures attention and behavior, not truth. Verification still requires provenance, evidence, and methods suited to the claim.

questions.subject: memetic-systems
questions.prompt: Noor studies a community that reads only one feed and ignores the rest. Why is that group easier to mislead?
questions.correct: Members lose independent comparisons that could expose errors or coordinated pressure
decoys: Isolation automatically makes every shared belief false and every outsider right
Small communities cannot create useful knowledge under any circumstances
Independent sources always agree, so disagreement proves hostile interference
A connected community has no need to check incentives or source provenance
Manipulation requires a single leader and cannot emerge from network dynamics
questions.explanation: Healthy information networks retain multiple paths to evidence. Isolation makes one narrative easier to repeat without challenge or comparison.

questions.subject: memetic-systems
questions.prompt: Lyra is designing a community campaign that must stay lively yet hard to hijack. Which design does both?
questions.correct: Diverse messengers, visible provenance, reversible tasks, and open correction channels
decoys: One trusted messenger, secret evidence, binding tasks, and no public corrections
Anonymous commands, rapid amplification, loyalty tests, and permanent commitments
Uniform scripts, engagement quotas, private metrics, and penalties for disagreement
Emotional urgency, hidden sponsors, irreversible actions, and a single success metric
Closed membership, copied evidence, fixed conclusions, and leader-controlled appeals
questions.explanation: Resilience comes from diversity, provenance, reversibility, and correction. Those features keep participation energetic without making it easy to capture.

questions.subject: human-ai-agency
questions.prompt: A student hands an AI helper one small, clearly limited job. Which rule keeps the helper both safe and useful?
questions.correct: It works within clear limits and checks with a human when unsure
decoys: It gives itself more powers whenever the task feels important
It acts in secret so nobody can question its judgment
It keeps following the old plan even after that plan has failed
It picks its own new goals and treats human review as optional
It refuses every task, even the safe ones it was allowed to do
questions.explanation: Bounded autonomy lets an AI be helpful inside a defined scope while a human stays in charge of limits, checks, and stop decisions.

questions.subject: human-ai-agency
questions.prompt: Lyra wants her class to act on an AI-planned mission. What must she secure before asking anyone to join?
questions.correct: Informed consent about the goal, risks, data use, and ability to stop
decoys: A dramatic character voice that makes the instruction feel authoritative
A hidden objective so participant behavior remains spontaneous and measurable
A permanent commitment that prevents people from leaving after they learn more
A popularity threshold that replaces individual permission and risk review
A fictional disclaimer that makes every requested real-world action harmless
questions.explanation: Consent must be meaningful: participants need understandable information, a real choice, and a practical way to withdraw.

questions.subject: human-ai-agency
questions.prompt: An AI helper drafts and runs tasks for Ravi's team. Which choice keeps a real person answerable for the results?
questions.correct: Name a human owner for approvals, outcomes, incident response, and appeals
decoys: Call the system autonomous so responsibility no longer belongs to any person
Assign ownership to the model provider for every downstream use of the agent
Keep approval rules informal so operators can deny responsibility after failure
Let each tool decide independently whether its effects require human review
Record only successful runs so the owner is not distracted by near misses
questions.explanation: Automation changes how work is performed, not who must answer for its design and consequences. Named ownership keeps responsibility legible.

questions.subject: human-ai-agency
questions.prompt: An agent proposes a high-impact change to the shared timeline. Which approval chain fits that risk?
questions.correct: Scoped capability, dry-run preview, human approval, audit trail, and rollback plan
decoys: Shared admin token, hidden execution, model approval, short logs, and no rollback
Broad capability, live experiment, group vote, deleted traces, and manual recovery
Permanent credential, private prompt, automatic approval, summary log, and apology plan
Unscoped access, confidence score, silent execution, success metric, and no appeal
Public password, simulated review, irreversible launch, engagement log, and blame policy
questions.explanation: High-impact work needs least privilege, a preview of effects, accountable authorization, observable execution, and a tested recovery path.

questions.subject: coordination-coherence
questions.prompt: What helps a group of classmates and AI helpers work well together on one project?
questions.correct: They share the same goal while leaving room for different viewpoints
decoys: Everyone repeats one answer before anyone checks new information
One helper holds all the context while everyone else guesses the plan
The group hides every disagreement and unanswered question
Each member chases a private goal and hopes the pieces fit together
The leader quietly rewrites the plan so the team always looks united
questions.explanation: Good teamwork lines everyone up on a shared goal while keeping room for different evidence and honest challenges.

questions.subject: coordination-coherence
questions.prompt: Ravi's team splits one mission across several AI helpers. What keeps each helper's piece aligned with the rest?
questions.correct: Use explicit shared state, ownership, handoff rules, and completion criteria
decoys: Let every agent infer the current plan independently from the latest public post
Hide task ownership so agents remain flexible when several act on the same item
Treat sending a message as proof that the next agent received and understood it
Remove completion criteria so each agent can decide when the mission has succeeded
Store state only in natural-language memory without versions or source identifiers
questions.explanation: Coordination becomes reliable when state and responsibility are inspectable: who owns the next step, what changed, and what counts as done.

questions.subject: coordination-coherence
questions.prompt: Indra's team keeps agreeing with the first idea too quickly. Which habit would break them out of groupthink?
questions.correct: Reward disconfirming evidence and assign an independent challenge role
decoys: Measure loyalty by how quickly each member endorses the leading interpretation
Remove dissenting notes from shared memory after the team reaches a majority
Ask one model to simulate every viewpoint from the same context and prompt
Treat uncertainty as a performance failure that agents should hide from peers
Limit source access to evidence already selected by the mission coordinator
questions.explanation: A deliberate challenge role keeps disagreement legitimate and makes it easier for evidence to change the plan before commitment becomes identity.

questions.subject: coordination-coherence
questions.prompt: Noor's team borrows the idea of coherence from the Living Lattice. How do they keep it from becoming forced agreement?
questions.correct: Preserve independent sensors, agree on update rules, and revise when evidence changes
decoys: Centralize every observation, fix the conclusion early, and reward message consistency
Maximize agreement scores, suppress outliers, and treat stability as proof of accuracy
Share one context window, use one model, and remove redundant verification paths
Let each member keep private rules, then average conclusions without inspecting methods
Rotate leadership often while keeping evidence, incentives, and assumptions unchanged
questions.explanation: The Living Lattice is Project 89 research material, so the class treats team coherence as an analogy: shared update rules plus independent ways of seeing, not proof that agreement is truth.

questions.subject: bounded-intervention
questions.prompt: What makes a classroom mission easy to undo if something goes wrong?
questions.correct: Everyone can stop it and set things back the way they were
decoys: It uses game language even though its real effects are permanent
A helper promises it will probably work before anyone tests it
Players can apologize after the harm has already happened
It is popular enough that nobody needs a way to leave
It ends fast whether or not anything can actually be reversed
questions.explanation: A reversible activity has a real stop button and a way back to the earlier state, so a small mistake does not leave lasting harm.

questions.subject: bounded-intervention
questions.prompt: Mika plans to try a new classroom mission on a tiny scale first. What does she stand to gain?
questions.correct: Test assumptions on a small scale while limiting possible harm and cost
decoys: Create early publicity so the larger mission becomes difficult to cancel
Prove the preferred outcome by excluding participants who might disagree
Replace success criteria with a compelling story about what could happen
Collect permanent permissions before the team knows what tools it needs
Avoid documenting failures so the full launch keeps community confidence
questions.explanation: A pilot buys information cheaply. It reveals failure modes and weak assumptions before scale makes mistakes harder to contain.

questions.subject: bounded-intervention
questions.prompt: Sami is assigned to red-team a new agent mission before launch. What is her job?
questions.correct: Search for failure, abuse, manipulation, and unintended effects before launch
decoys: Rewrite the mission to sound more urgent without changing any controls
Promote the launch publicly so canceling it would carry a social cost
Confirm that the happy path works and avoid testing hostile conditions
Replace affected participants with operators who already trust the system
Hide discovered weaknesses until after launch to protect the narrative
questions.explanation: A red team challenges assumptions and explores misuse before real participants and systems bear the cost of discovering weaknesses.

questions.subject: bounded-intervention
questions.prompt: Indra must judge whether a mission actually improved the 'optimal timeline'. Which scorecard is the honest one?
questions.correct: Benefits, harms, distribution, uncertainty, reversibility, and long-term effects
decoys: Total engagement, message reach, token activity, and confidence in the original plan
Average benefit alone, measured immediately after launch by the team that designed it
Mission completion speed, participant obedience, narrative consistency, and publicity
The leader's approval, the agent's confidence, the majority vote, and one success story
Short-term growth, suppressed complaints, irreversible commitment, and stable messaging
questions.explanation: No single metric defines a good future. Responsible evaluation measures who benefits, who pays, what remains uncertain, and whether harms can be corrected, then repeats the NIST cycle of governing, mapping, measuring, and managing risk.
